namespace.why: This repository already holds at least eight incompatible curriculum naming schemes and the last thing it needs is a ninth. Three surfaces built concurrently spell the M1 Codex cards this way: `codexCardIds` in packages/curriculum/src/conceptRegistry.ts, `codexCardIds` on every concept card of the module deck in content/m1/module.json, and the item `codexCardIds` in content/m1/duel-items.json. This file adopts the spelling unchanged and supplies the one thing the others do not — what each card actually says.
namespace.structuralNote: The mission segment `MD01` is inherited from §4.9 and is a known wart. packages/curriculum/src/types.ts deliberately dropped the mission segment from CONCEPT ids because a spiral concept cannot belong to mission day one, and the same argument applies to a card. Renaming the cards to `BOS.CARD.*` is the right end state and is a multi-file change (this file, the registry, the module deck, the duel bank, and cardIdentity.ts). It is not done here because a rename that lands in one of those files is worse than the wart.
namespace.conceptIdsUsed: Canonical, from packages/curriculum. Each card carries the legacy learner id too, so a consumer that has not adopted the registry yet still resolves.

lifecycle.learnedAt: Set when the student completes the module that sources the card. Every card below is sourced by exactly one module card, so 'learned' is a fact about the deck rather than a judgement about the student.
lifecycle.pvpLegalAt: Minted only at 100% mastery of the card's concept on the chapter capstone. No duel result and no mission clear may set it. A student can hold all nine of these cards as learned, clear M1 on the first attempt, and still have none of them PvP-legal.
lifecycle.whatTheCodexIsFor: The Codex is the index of what a player can be asked. Facing a question whose card you do not hold means you probably miss it, fight that round on the wrong-answer grant, and go learn it. Cards are never played as a deck.
lifecycle.mintedByThisMission: Nothing. M1 mints no cards; duel performance is evidence rather than a granting event.

rescopeNote: REWRITTEN 2026-07-30 for the 1774 Coercive-Acts slate. The three REPRESENTATION cards below are unchanged — they are the strongest assets in the repo and the consent concept survives the rescope intact. The six INTOLERABLE_ACTS and MERCANTILISM cards replaced the retired POSTWAR_REVENUE and STAMP_SCOPE cards (three each). The known CONSENT_GROUND vs LAWFUL_NOT_CONSENTED confusability is handled in the duel-item stems (SPEAKS_FOR_ALL and LAWFUL_BUT_UNJUST both name Parliament's speaks-for-everyone claim), not by rewording the cards.

cards.title: The closure is a punishment
cards.proposition: Parliament's answer to the destroyed tea was to close the whole harbour, not to fine or try the men who did it. Because the Port Act shuts the port itself, it falls on every trade in Boston — the fishmonger and the ropemaker who never touched the tea starve beside those who did. This card is the NATURE of the act: collective punishment aimed at a town, guilty and innocent together. It is not the list of the four acts, and not what they leave lawful.
cards.note: The most load-bearing proposition of the mission: 41-43% of students (2021 #38, 2022 #4) read the coercive acts as ordinary governance rather than as punishment aimed at a whole town.

cards.title: Four acts, not one
cards.proposition: The Coercive Acts are four, and each does a different thing. The Port Act shut the harbour. The Massachusetts Government Act rewrote the charter and ended the town meetings. The Quartering Act put soldiers in the town. The Administration of Justice Act moved trials out of reach, out of a Boston jury's hands. This card is the SCOPE of the four acts: which act did what. It is not the fact that the closure is a punishment, and not the reading of what they leave alone.
cards.note: The concept was authored to let items 'distinguish the four acts from one another' rather than treat 'Intolerable Acts' as one undifferentiated label; these items do exactly that.

cards.title: What the Acts do not forbid
cards.proposition: Read what is NOT in the four acts. The port is shut and the assembly banned, but walking a street with printed paper in your hand is still lawful — the Acts forbade the harbour, the meeting and the sheltering of trials, not the carrying of a sheet. This card is the LEGAL BOUNDARY of the Acts, and it is what makes a print-shop runner's cover hold: the courier breaks no law by carrying the pledge through the town. It is not the scope of what each act prohibits, and not the punishment's reach.
cards.note: Load-bearing for the mission's own fiction: the player talks past patrols with this exact proposition, so knowing precisely what was prohibited is what protects them.

cards.title: No vote in Parliament
cards.proposition: Boston elects its own town meeting and its own members of the Massachusetts assembly, but it elects no member of the Parliament that laid this tax. This card is the plain fact of who Boston does and does not choose. It is not the principle that makes the fact matter, and not the reply to London's defence.

cards.title: Only the chosen may tax
cards.proposition: A tax is legitimate only when it is laid by a body the taxed people chose; the objection is to who laid it, not to what it costs — Boston would say the same if the stamp cost a farthing. This card is the principle. It is not the bare fact of Boston's missing vote, and not the answer to the claim that Parliament already speaks for everyone.
cards.note: The most load-bearing card in the mission and the one most often half-held: students reliably reach the objection and land it on the price. The strongest single asset in the repo — it states the correct answer of the hardest measured item almost verbatim.

cards.title: Lawful is not consent
cards.proposition: London's defence is that Parliament already speaks for every subject, voted for or not — 'virtual representation.' Boston's reply: a lawful vote taken by men the town never chose is still not the town's consent. This card is the answer to that one claim. It is not the general principle, and not the bare fact of the missing vote.
cards.note: CONSENT_GROUND and this card are a confusable pair — a principle and its rebuttal. They separate only when the question invokes Parliament's speaks-for-everyone claim, so SPEAKS_FOR_ALL and LAWFUL_BUT_UNJUST name it in the stem.

cards.title: They stop buying
cards.proposition: The colonists cannot declare war and cannot tax London, so what they do is stop buying. Merchants sign an agreement not to import British goods — non-importation — and the pledge the courier carries, the Solemn League and Covenant, is exactly that agreement. This card is the FORM the answer takes: withholding trade rather than making it. It is not the reason the withholding works, and not the boundary against war and counter-taxation.
cards.note: 37% of students confuse the boycott with taxing British imports back; the concept exists to hold the line between withholding trade and counter-taxing it.

cards.title: A congress, not an army
cards.proposition: The forms of resistance are lawful ones: the towns petition, and a congress meets to coordinate the colonies and agree the boycott together. A congress petitions and organises; it does not raise an army or declare a war. This card is the PEACEFUL machinery of the answer — petition and congress — beside the boycott itself. It is not non-importation proper, and not the boundary against the wrong forms.
cards.note: 28% of students think the First Continental Congress declared war; the concept holds that a congress coordinates and petitions rather than fights.

cards.title: Neither war nor a tax of their own
cards.proposition: Two things the colonists do NOT do. They do not declare war — not in 1774; a congress petitions rather than fights. And they cannot lay a tax of their own on British goods, because they have no power to tax London's trade. This card is the BOUNDARY of the answer: it names the two wrong forms the measured errors reach for, so that 'stop buying' is understood against 'declare war' and 'tax them back'. It is not the boycott itself, and not the congress that agrees it.
cards.note: The card authored directly against the two most common wrong answers: the congress declaring war (28%) and the colonies taxing British imports (37%).
